chapter: Mutes, influences and the blues singers
title: Ethel Waters calls him on stage to play 'Am I Blue?'
summary: In Philadelphia Ethel Waters asked her favourite trumpeter in the audience to join her; he borrowed a pit trumpet and used what he learned from Dyer.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them
story.community_name: Bessie, Mamie, Ma Rainey: the classic blues queens

blocks.x: How about a blues singer whose name wasn't Smith? Who do you recall are the great ones, that you knew personally?
I'm trying to think right now (inaudible). I knew plenty of them, but I'm trying to think what names.
Well now for example, Ethel Waters, I think you knew Ethel Waters when she was something else again.
Oh, ho, ho, oh. You'd better believe
it. I played for her so many times. Bessie was something else. I mean Ethel.

Yeah, she was -- oh man, what -- and the thing that knocked me out, I was sitting in the theater one night, digging her show. I was in Philadelphia, by the way. She was there with the show -- no, she was there and somebody called out in the audience and sort of come up on stage and be acknowledged and do a number, so they asked her to sing "Am I Blue?" And sure. And she said, "Well, I would love to do it for you," only she's always been such a lady, and she said, "But if I can get -- I happen to see one of my favorite trumpet players sitting in the audience. If he will come up and join me and play for me -- " That was me!

Oooooh! And this was not planned. Boy, and I -- that had never happened to me before. You know? So I think -- and the guy in the pit loaned me his trumpet, and went up on the stage. (Sings) 'Am I blue? Wah wah wah. Lah dah dee. Blah blah blah. Then all that I'd learned from Dyer came back to me, and I was thinking about her while I was playing, and playing for Ethel. And it really -- really paid off, and made me feel very, very good. You know?
